clue.text: Join the commuters with abandon

parts.note: the phrase for heading into the city centre with the daily travellers also means acting without restraint, throwing oneself into something

explanation.surface: An invitation to leave home behind and travel in with the rush-hour crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The commuters' trip into the city and the idiom for doing something lavishly share one four-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Commuters travel into the city each day, and the same idiom means to do something lavishly or with gusto.

clue.text: Successful old leader of the band employing 300 trumpeters!

definitions.text: Successful old leader of the band employing 300 trumpeters!

parts.words: Successful old leader of the band employing 300 trumpeters!
parts.note: the biblical judge who routed the Midianites with three hundred men blowing trumpets, described as if he led a brass band

explanation.surface: Praise for a veteran bandleader with an enormous brass section.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Judges this leader defeated the Midianites with 300 men who blew trumpets and smashed jars; 'band' means his troop, not musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Old Testament this judge led a chosen force of three hundred men, each with a trumpet, to victory.

clue.text: It acknowledges a hit even without its extremities

definitions.text: It acknowledges a hit even without its extremities

parts.words: It acknowledges a hit even without its extremities
parts.note: the fencer's cry conceding a hit; strip its first and last letters and what is left is the cry of someone who has been hurt

explanation.surface: A fencer admits a hit, even one landed without arms or legs.
explanation.walkthrough: The fencer's word conceding a hit, with first and last letters removed, leaves OUCH, which also acknowledges a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: In fencing this French word is called out to admit an opponent's hit, and in argument to concede a good point.

clue.text: Illuminating for the board, but it's not up to standard

definitions.text: Illuminating for the board, but it's not up to standard

parts.words: Illuminating for the board, but it's not up to standard
parts.note: a light that stands on a board (a table), shorter than the tall floor-standing kind called a standard

explanation.surface: A report found enlightening by the directors yet below the required quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' is a table, not directors, and a 'standard' is a tall floor lamp, so this light is not up to that height.
explanation.definitionFit: A small light stands on a table, while a standard lamp is the tall floor version.

clue.text: Garments that twist twisters !

parts.note: to wind is to twist or coil
a twister is a swindler, a cheat

explanation.surface: A tongue-twister about clothes that spin around tornadoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisters' suggests tornadoes; in British slang a twister is a crook, so it gives CHEATERS.
explanation.definitionFit: These are windproof jackets, outer garments made to keep out the breeze.

clue.text: Falsely accused of being "only a beautiful picture?…'

definitions.text: Falsely accused of being "only a beautiful picture?

parts.words: Falsely accused of being "only a beautiful picture?
parts.note: a person set up by false evidence and a painting hung in a border are described by the same word

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being dismissed as merely a pretty face on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: A picture is put in a border before hanging; a person stitched up with planted evidence gets the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be set up by fabricated evidence is to be stitched up, and a picture placed in a mount and border is likewise fitted out.

clue.text: All Burma turns out for a dance

indicators.note: the letters turn out differently, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: The whole of Burma comes out to dance.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively ballroom dance originated in Cuba.

clue.text: It helps one remember the wild men with a Scot in charge

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of men are scrambled

parts.note: mon is the Scots form of man, used as a word for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: Wild men led by a Scotsman help someone recall something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' turns MEN into MNE; MON is the Scots pronunciation of 'man'.
explanation.definitionFit: A memory aid such as a rhyme or acronym is designed to help people recall facts.

clue.text: Is it time for all good men to leave the country ?

definitions.text: Is it time for all good men to leave the country ?

parts.words: Is it time for all good men to leave the country ?
parts.note: read as a brain-drain era, a time when talent flows away; also the draining of water from land

explanation.surface: A gloomy question about emigration, playing on the typing-practice phrase about good men.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as DRAIN AGE: a 'brain drain' era when the best people emigrate. 'Country' also means land, which gets its water drained off.
explanation.definitionFit: The removal of surplus water from land is the drawing-off of water from the countryside.

clue.text: Cheap massage takes some beating

parts.note: something cheap costs a penny, and D is the old abbreviation for a penny
a massage is a rubbing of the body

explanation.surface: A bargain-price massage turns out to be a painful pummelling.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the abbreviation for the old British penny (from Latin denarius), so a 'cheap' massage is a penny rub.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing is a heavy defeat or beating, so 'some beating' describes a sound trouncing.

clue.text: Changing form of the Simple Life

definitions.text: Changing form of the Simple Life

parts.words: Changing form of the Simple Life
parts.note: a single-celled organism, a simple form of life, that keeps altering its shape as it moves

explanation.surface: Sounds like a review of a lifestyle magazine that has gone back to basics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Simple Life' suggests a rustic lifestyle; read literally it is a primitive life form whose body has no fixed shape.
explanation.definitionFit: This single-celled organism is among the simplest living things and constantly reshapes itself with pseudopodia.

clue.text: Type of stock that may need watering

definitions.text: Type of stock that may need watering

parts.words: Type of stock that may need watering
parts.note: a garden flower called stock whose variety is fragrant after dark; a plant needs water, and so might shares or livestock

explanation.surface: Advice about cattle or company shares that need watering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' suggests livestock or shares (watered stock is a finance term); here it is the garden flower of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: This variety of the garden flower stock releases its fragrance in the evening.

clue.text: A colourful chore when reorganized

indicators.note: reorganizing something puts its parts in a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finds a dull household task brightens up once it is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellowish-brown earth pigment names a colour, so it serves as a colouring adjective.

clue.text: Urban quarter in the Potteries ?

parts.note: the Potteries towns of Staffordshire make porcelain, so a district there is a porcelain town; the phrase also names a Chinese district in a city

explanation.surface: A question about which neighbourhood of a Staffordshire city is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Potteries are the six towns of Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, England, famous for making porcelain; a city's Chinese district takes the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Many big cities have a district settled by Chinese immigrants, and the Potteries' towns are literally porcelain towns.

clue.text: Daily execution of house improvement ?

parts.note: a daily is a newspaper, so it gives paper
hanging is a form of execution

explanation.surface: A grim newspaper report of a hanging, dressed up as home improvement.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting up wallpaper is a common way to improve a home's rooms.

clue.text: Of course it's only half!

parts.note: a golf course usually has eighteen holes, so half a round is that number halved

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something is obviously only half done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' sounds like 'naturally'; it means 'of a golf course', which has eighteen holes, so half is nine.
explanation.definitionFit: A full golf round is eighteen holes, so half of a course is the short round of nine.

clue.text: Copper with a record, competent but guilty

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
an LP is a long-playing record
able means competent

explanation.surface: A capable police officer with a criminal record is still to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer with a criminal record; it is the chemical symbol CU, and the record is a vinyl LP.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone deserving blame for wrongdoing is blameworthy, at fault.

clue.text: Sound sort of agent to give a puss a roll

indicators.note: Sound tells us the word is identified by how it is pronounced

parts.note: a puss is a cat, and a roll is a list (a roll-call), so this says cat a list

explanation.surface: An odd recipe for an agent: roll the cat over.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, CAT A LIST matches the answer. 'Roll' means a list of names, not tumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry, a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up is a reaction agent.

clue.text: Piping a tune's all wrong in effect for a gourmet !

indicators.note: letters that are all wrong are out of their proper order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A diner complains that the piped music in a restaurant puts a food lover off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piping' suggests piping hot food; it is part of the anagram fodder with A and TUNES, which 'all wrong' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Something whose effect on a food connoisseur is off-putting is unpalatable to them.

clue.text: Do a favour to an old boy with one leg broken !

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

indicators.note: a broken leg is out of shape, so its letters with I are rearranged

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A kindness done for a former schoolboy who has broken a leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' looks like part of the surface injury; it is the anagram signal, acting on 'one' and 'leg' together, not on 'leg' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To help someone out by doing something for them is to accommodate them.

clue.text: Theatre parts that only go part of the way

definitions.text: only go part of the way

explanation.surface: A comment on theatrical roles that are left unfinished.
explanation.definitionFit: Platforms where plays are performed are parts of a theatre, and legs of a journey cover only some of the distance.

clue.text: Its seedlings should get off to a flying start !

definitions.text: Its seedlings should get off to a flying start !

parts.words: Its seedlings should get off to a flying start !
parts.note: an aircraft takes off flying, and this tree's name begins with the word for an aircraft

explanation.surface: A gardener hopes young plants will establish themselves quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree's name opens with a word for an aircraft, so its seedlings literally start with something that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: This large broad-leaved tree, common in London streets, shares its first word with an aircraft.

clue.text: Feature of balance sheet to which one takes exception ?

definitions.text: Feature of balance sheet to which one takes exception ?

parts.words: Feature of balance sheet to which one takes exception ?
parts.note: invoices often say mistakes and omissions excepted, so the accountant takes exception to such a slip in a formal sense

explanation.surface: An auditor objects to an item in the company accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Accounts and invoices print 'E&OE', 'errors and omissions excepted', so a slip is literally something excepted.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake is something that is formally excepted on accounts and that people object to.

clue.text: But Lady Godiva did not make this of riding without it

definitions.text: But Lady Godiva did not make this of riding without it

parts.words: But Lady Godiva did not make this of riding without it
parts.note: a rider's outfit and a regular practice share one word; Godiva rode naked once, so it was no regular practice to ride without the outfit

explanation.surface: A remark on the legendary naked ride through Coventry by Lady Godiva.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Godiva is said to have ridden naked through Coventry, England, once. A riding outfit and a regular practice share the word: she did not 'make a ___ of' riding without one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a rider's traditional costume and a settled routine, as in making something a regular practice.

clue.text: Scholar returns the cart to get the horse

parts.note: a BA (Bachelor of Arts) is a graduate scholar

indicators.note: returns means the word for the cart is read backwards

parts.note: a dray is a low heavy cart, as used by brewers

explanation.surface: A scholar gives back the cart and takes the horse instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns DRAY into YARD. Bayard is the magical bay horse of medieval French legend.
explanation.definitionFit: In chivalric romance this is the famous magic steed of Renaud, and the name came to stand for any horse.

clue.text: Playing for time ? Stone-walling ? Nothing new in this !

indicators.note: the clue says there is nothing new in this word, so those letters are removed from it

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator remarks that defensive time-wasting batting is an old tactic.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove O (nothing) and NEW from STONEWALLING. Stonewalling, blocking every ball, is also a cricket term for defensive batting.
explanation.definitionFit: Delaying tactics used to gain time are a way of holding off, or temporizing.

clue.text: Was it only formerly wrong for governments to get money thus ?

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-husband
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: A political question whether governments once wrongly squeezed money from citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thus' points back to the wordplay: getting money in a way that is a former-wrong, EX + TORT.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain money by force or threats is to wring it out of someone, which is what the word means.

clue.text: Homer's homer

parts.note: the hero of the poet Homer's epic, who spends ten years trying to get home, like a homing pigeon

explanation.surface: Two words about the ancient Greek poet and his hero.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'homer' is a homing pigeon; the hero of Homer's Odyssey spends the poem making his way home to Ithaca.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Homer's Odyssey struggles for ten years to return to his home in Ithaca.
